question: In anammox, ammonium is oxidized without O2. Which compound acts as the electron acceptor?
options: Nitrate
Nitrite
Sulfate
Ferric iron
explain: Anammox bacteria combine ammonium and nitrite into N2 and water (NH4+ + NO2− → N2 + 2 H2O). One nitrogen atom of each N2 comes from ammonium and the other from nitrite.

statement: Methanogenesis, as a way of conserving energy, is known from both Bacteria and Archaea.
explain: No known bacterium conserves energy by methanogenesis; the methanogens described so far are archaea. Bacteria contribute by fermenting organic matter to the H2, CO2, formate and acetate that methanogens use.

question: Match each CAZy class with what its members do.

pairs.right: Form glycosidic bonds from activated sugar donors
Cleave uronic acid-containing chains by β-elimination
Remove ester-linked groups such as acetyl from sugars
Bind carbohydrates without catalysing a reaction

explain: These are the main classes of the CAZy database, which tools such as dbCAN use to annotate genomes. CAZy also has an Auxiliary Activities (AA) class of redox enzymes, such as lytic polysaccharide monooxygenases, that help break down polysaccharides and lignin.

question: Why do nitrifying bacteria need reverse electron flow to make NADH?
options: Their electron donors have more positive reduction potentials than NAD+/NADH, so reducing NAD+ costs proton motive force
Their electron donors have more negative reduction potentials than NAD+/NADH, so NAD+ would be over-reduced
They have no electron transport chain, so electrons must pass back through glycolysis
Their terminal electron acceptor is nitrate, which returns electrons to the donor
explain: Ammonia and nitrite give up electrons at potentials well above that of NAD+/NADH (−0.32 V). Nitrifiers spend part of their proton motive force to push some electrons uphill, through the quinone pool and a reversed complex I, to reduce NAD+.

statement: Soluble methane monooxygenase contains copper, so methanotrophs make it mainly when copper is plentiful.
explain: Soluble MMO has a di-iron active site and is made when copper is scarce. When copper is available, methanotrophs switch to particulate MMO, a copper enzyme in the membrane; this copper switch is well studied in Methylococcus and Methylosinus.

question: Match each marker gene used in genome annotation with the enzyme it encodes.
explain: These genes mark nitrogen fixation, nitrification, methanogenesis (and anaerobic methane oxidation), sulfate reduction and denitrification. Finding one shows genetic potential rather than activity, and dsrA also occurs in some sulfur oxidizers, which run the Dsr pathway in reverse.

question: A bacterial genome lacks the genes for cobalamin (vitamin B12) synthesis. It encodes the B12-dependent methionine synthase MetH but not the B12-independent enzyme MetE. In a defined medium without methionine, what does it need in order to grow?
options: Cobalt ions, so it can assemble B12 itself
Molybdenum, which serves as the MetH cofactor
Folate only, since MetH needs no other cofactor
Vitamin B12, from the medium or another organism
explain: MetH moves a methyl group from methyl-tetrahydrofolate to homocysteine through bound methylcobalamin, so it cannot work without B12. With no B12 synthesis genes and no MetE, the cell can make methionine only from imported B12, a common dependency in microbial communities.

question: dbCAN assigns a protein from a new soil isolate to glycoside hydrolase family GH5. What can you conclude from this alone?
options: It is a cellulase, since GH5 enzymes act on cellulose
It is an α-amylase, since GH5 enzymes act on starch
It shares the GH5 fold and mechanism, but its substrate is not yet known
It is a glycosyltransferase, since GH5 enzymes build cell walls
explain: CAZy families are defined by sequence similarity, so members share a fold and catalytic mechanism but can differ in substrate. GH5 is large and polyspecific, including cellulases, mannanases and xylanases, so CAZy subfamilies, neighbouring genes or experiments are needed to pin down the activity.

statement: Cyanobacteria use two photosystems linked in series, whereas each anoxygenic phototroph uses a single type of reaction centre.
explain: In the cyanobacterial Z scheme, photosystem II oxidizes water and photosystem I reduces ferredoxin and NADP+. Anoxygenic phototrophs have either a quinone-type (type II) or an iron–sulfur (type I) reaction centre, and no single reaction centre spans the gap from water to ferredoxin.

scenario: A metagenome-assembled genome from a sulfide-rich, anoxic lake layer encodes ATP citrate lyase, 2-oxoglutarate:ferredoxin oxidoreductase and pyruvate:ferredoxin oxidoreductase, but no RubisCO or phosphoribulokinase. It also carries genes for chlorosome proteins and a type I (iron–sulfur) reaction centre.

parts.question: Which carbon fixation pathway does this genome most likely use?
options: The Calvin cycle
The Wood–Ljungdahl pathway
The reverse citric acid cycle
The 3-hydroxypropionate bi-cycle
parts.explain: ATP citrate lyase and the two ferredoxin-dependent carboxylating oxidoreductases are hallmarks of the reverse citric acid cycle. The lack of RubisCO and phosphoribulokinase rules out the Calvin cycle.

parts.question: Which group does the genome most likely belong to?
options: Green sulfur bacteria (Chlorobi)
Purple sulfur bacteria (Chromatiaceae)
Cyanobacteria
Heliobacteria
parts.explain: Chlorosomes, a type I reaction centre and the reverse citric acid cycle together match green sulfur bacteria such as Chlorobium. Purple sulfur bacteria and cyanobacteria use the Calvin cycle, and heliobacteria have a type I reaction centre but no chlorosomes.

parts.question: The lake layer has no O2. Why does this suit the genome's carbon fixation pathway?
options: The pathway uses O2 to regenerate oxaloacetate
Its ferredoxin-dependent carboxylating enzymes are damaged by O2
Its RubisCO reacts with O2 in place of CO2
Its chlorosomes need O2 to assemble
parts.explain: 2-Oxoglutarate:ferredoxin and pyruvate:ferredoxin oxidoreductases are sensitive to O2. This helps explain why the reverse citric acid cycle is found in anaerobes and microaerophiles, such as green sulfur bacteria and Aquificae.

explain: Reading carbon fixation and photosynthesis genes together places this genome among the green sulfur bacteria. Their reverse citric acid cycle suits anoxic, sulfidic habitats where reduced ferredoxin is plentiful.
